Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impression:  
  - Acute onset (~3 hours) chest tightness described as inability to take a full breath, mild shortness of breath (worse on exertion/stairs, not at rest), wheeze and non‑productive cough following a recent upper respiratory infection.  
  - Known history of atopic asthma with prior severe exacerbation requiring intubation in adolescence.  
  - Medication omission: has been without inhaled steroid (Clenil) and salbutamol for ~1 week.  
  - No vitals, oxygen saturation, peak flow, or physical exam findings recorded to objectively grade severity.  

- Working diagnosis (supported by transcript and DDx):  
  - Acute asthma exacerbation (infective and/or allergic trigger), High likelihood.  
    - Justification: known asthma, acute wheeze and cough after recent URTI, typical nocturnal/exertional worsening, and documented omission of inhaled steroid and reliever for ~1 week; aligns with DDx top-ranked diagnosis.

- Plan documented in transcript:  
  - Prescriptions to be sent for inhalers: salbutamol (Ventolin) and Clenil Modulite (inhaled steroid) — dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  - Oral corticosteroid prescribed: "two tablets in the morning for five days" — steroid name and dose per tablet not documented.  
  - Spacer to be provided with instructions on use.  
  - Advice: use Ventolin PRN; seek medical attention if using Ventolin more frequently than every three hours or if worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, light-headedness, or other concerning deterioration.  
  - Time off work suggested/self-certify first seven days; advised to rest.  
  - No objective monitoring (peak flow, O2 sat) or formal follow-up appointment documented.  

- Relevant differentials from DDx that refine the clinician’s impression:  
  - Viral bronchitis / post-viral reactive airways (Medium likelihood): recent URTI with persistent cough and wheeze could represent post‑viral airway hyperreactivity; may coexist with asthma exacerbation.  
  - Community-acquired pneumonia (Low–Medium likelihood): possible post‑viral bacterial infection but absence of fever, productive cough, focal chest pain or focal findings reduces likelihood.  
  - Pulmonary embolism and primary cardiac causes considered in DDx but judged unlikely given young age, wheeze-predominant history and no supporting features; to be reconsidered if clinical course changes.  
  - Anxiety/hyperventilation (Low likelihood) may contribute to symptom perception but objective wheeze and asthma history favor physiological airway disease.  

- Considerations (additional plausible but uncertain options from DDx):  
  - Consider post-viral reactive airways/bronchitis as a coexisting or precipitating factor.  
  - Consider secondary bacterial infection (pneumonia) if fever, focal chest signs, or sputum production develop.  
  - Consider alternative diagnoses (PE, cardiac) only if clinical features evolve inconsistent with asthma or do not respond to initial therapy.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- 1) Acute asthma exacerbation — High likelihood.  
  - Justification: Known asthma with prior severe exacerbation; acute wheeze, cough and chest tightness after recent URTI; documented omission of inhaled steroid and salbutamol for ~1 week — all strongly point to asthma exacerbation.

- 2) Viral bronchitis / post-viral reactive airways — Medium likelihood.  
  - Justification: Recent cold with persistent non-productive cough and wheeze could represent a post-viral reactive airway process, particularly in an atopic patient.

- 3) Community-acquired pneumonia — Low to Medium likelihood.  
  - Justification: Possible after URTI but absence of fever, productive sputum, focal chest pain or focal exam findings reduces likelihood; consider if clinical course changes.
